505.title: Nothing is impossible (Luke 1:26–38)
505.hook: Mary asks how, and hears: with God nothing shall be impossible
505.howItsDone: Many churches celebrate the Annunciation on March 25, nine months before Christmas; Catholic and Orthodox Christians pray the Hail Mary, which begins with Gabriel's greeting, and many Christians read this passage in Advent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zechariah was struck silent, and Elisabeth kept her joy hidden for five months. Your line was silence can grow things. Where did you say less, and what grew? Day five hundred five.

In the sixth month of Elisabeth's pregnancy, Luke says, the same angel is sent somewhere completely different. Not the capital, not the holy place, not to a priest. To Nazareth, a village in Galilee the Old Testament never mentions. To a young woman named Mary, engaged to a man named Joseph, of the house of David. Luke doesn't tell us her age, or what she was doing when the angel came in. Cooking, maybe. Fetching water. Ordinary hours in an ordinary house. Yesterday an old priest in a golden room. Today a girl in a village nobody's heard of. And the message she's about to receive is far stranger than his.

Gabriel's greeting, in the King James Bible: "Hail, thou that art highly favoured, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women." Luke says she was troubled, and turned the words over in her mind, wondering what kind of greeting this was. Then the news: she will bear a son, she'll name him Jesus, and he will be called the Son of the Highest, and his kingdom will have no end. Mary asks a question: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" Notice the difference from Zechariah. He asked, how can I be sure? She asks, how will this happen? Not proof. Just how. And Gabriel answers: the Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee. Then he gives her a sign she can go and see for herself: your relative Elisabeth, the one everybody called barren, is six months along. And then the line: "For with God nothing shall be impossible." In Greek, it can also be read as no word from God will be without power. God's promises don't fall to the ground. And Mary's answer: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word." Then the angel leaves. Christians across the churches treasure this scene, and they honor Mary in different ways. Catholic and Orthodox Christians honor her with special devotion as the Mother of God; the Hail Mary prayer opens with Gabriel's greeting. Many Protestant Christians honor her as a model of trusting faith. All of them hear a yes in her last line: be it unto me.
screen: `BE IT UNTO ME ACCORDING TO THY WORD.`
then, large: `WITH GOD NOTHING SHALL BE IMPOSSIBLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bring one impossible thing to God. Settle, and breathe. Think of something in your life that looks impossible. A relationship that seems beyond repair. An illness. A habit you can't break. Someone you love who seems unreachable. Don't pretend it's easy. Mary didn't; she asked how. Just hold the impossible thing, honestly, the way you'd hold something heavy in both hands. Then, if you can, loosen your grip a little. If you pray, you can bring it to God, and if the words fit, say Mary's line: be it unto me according to thy word. If you don't, simply hold it open, without forcing an answer. The bell holds the time.
Gabriel. The angel who told Mary that with God nothing is impossible, and that no word from him lacks power.
Your line: be it unto me. Today, when you hear yourself say that'll never happen, pause and ask Mary's question instead: how might this be? Day five hundred five.

506.title: He has filled the hungry (Luke 1:39–56)
506.hook: Mary's song turns the world upside down, and Luke's whole gospel will follow it
506.howItsDone: The Magnificat is sung or said daily in several traditions: at Vespers in the Catholic Church, at Evening Prayer or Evensong in Anglican churches, and at the morning service in Orthodox churches; some Christians also connect it with feeding the hungry.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mary's yes, and Gabriel's promise that with God nothing is impossible. Your line was be it unto me. What impossible thing did you hold, and did asking how change anything? Day five hundred six.

Mary doesn't stay home with her news. Luke says she went with haste into the hill country of Judah, to the house of Zechariah, to see Elisabeth, the sign the angel gave her. A young woman, newly pregnant, goes to an older relative, the one people called barren, now six months along. Two unlikely mothers under one roof. Mary steps through the door and greets her. And before anyone says anything else, the baby inside Elisabeth jumps. Luke says the babe leaped in her womb. Some readers say John, not yet born, is already doing his job: pointing.

Elisabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, cries out: "Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb." And then Mary sings. In the King James Bible her song begins: "My soul doth magnify the Lord, And my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour." In Latin the first word is Magnificat, and that's the name the song carries. It starts personal: God has looked on me, a lowly servant. But then it widens, and it turns the world upside down. "He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree. He hath filled the hungry with good things; and the rich he hath sent empty away." Thrones emptied, the humble lifted, hungry people fed, rich people sent off with nothing. Mary sings it in the past tense, as if it's already happened. It echoes an older song, sung by Hannah in the book of Samuel, another woman who praised God for a child and for the world turned over. And here's why Luke puts it right at the start: his whole Gospel follows this song. Again and again in Luke, the poor are lifted and the comfortable are unsettled. Later, Jesus will say, in Luke's version of his sermon: "Blessed are ye that hunger now: for ye shall be filled." Mary's song is the overture, and the rest of the book plays its tune. Catholic Vespers and Anglican Evensong still sing or say it each evening. Some hear it mostly as a song about God's mercy to the humble heart. Others also hear it as a call to feed the hungry, here and now. Mary's song, still sung as the day ends.
screen: then, large: `HE HATH FILLED THE HUNGRY WITH GOOD THINGS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give food to the hungry. Settle, and breathe. Think about where hunger is close to you. A neighbor living alone. A food bank in your town. A student who skips lunch. A coworker who's broke until payday. Someone on the corner you pass every day. Picture a face, if you can. Then picture a plate of good things, the way Mary sang it, not scraps, good things, set in front of them. Decide on one real thing you'll do: drop groceries at a food bank, buy someone lunch, give to a meal program, cook extra and share. If you pray, you can offer that act to God as part of Mary's song. If you don't, simply make the plan. The bell holds the time.
Magnificat, the name of Mary's song, from its first Latin word, magnify: she sings that God lifts the lowly and fills the hungry with good things.
Your line: the hungry filled. Today, put good food in front of someone who needs it, and don't make them thank you for it. Day five hundred six.

what it means: a young woman sings that God puts down the mighty, lifts the lowly and fills the hungry, as if it's already done.

507.title: His name is John (Luke 1:57–80)
507.hook: Zechariah's tongue loosens into a song: the dayspring from on high
507.howItsDone: The Benedictus is sung or said each morning in several traditions: at Lauds in the Catholic Liturgy of the Hours and at Morning Prayer in Anglican and Lutheran traditions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mary's song: he has filled the hungry with good things. Your line was the hungry filled. Who did you put good food in front of? Day five hundred seven.

Eight days after the baby is born, the house is full. Neighbors, cousins, the whole extended family, there for the circumcision and the naming. Everybody has an opinion, and everybody agrees: name him Zechariah, after his father. Obviously. Then Elisabeth speaks up: "Not so; but he shall be called John." The relatives push back. Nobody in your family has that name. So they turn to the father, still silent after all these months, and make signs to ask him. And Zechariah, the old priest who couldn't say a word, asks for a writing tablet.
screen: `EIGHT DAYS: A HOUSE FULL OF OPINIONS.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "he asked for a writing table, and wrote, saying, His name is John. And they marvelled all." Not his name will be John. His name is John. It's already settled; the angel named him months ago. And in that moment of trust, "his mouth was opened immediately, and his tongue loosed, and he spake, and praised God." Months of silence, and the first thing out of him is praise, and then a song. In Latin it begins Benedictus, blessed, and that's its name. "Blessed be the Lord God of Israel; for he hath visited and redeemed his people." The first half is about all of Israel, God keeping old promises to Abraham and David. Then the old man turns to the child, and the song turns tender: "And thou, child, shalt be called the prophet of the Highest: for thou shalt go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways." Imagine being eight days old and hearing your job description. And then these lines: "whereby the dayspring from on high hath visited us, To give light to them that sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace." Dayspring is an old English word for sunrise, the first light. Christians hear in it Jesus, the light John will point toward. Behind dayspring is the Greek word anatole, a rising. Some readers notice that the old Greek version of the prophets uses the same word for the promised branch from David's line. A sunrise, and a new shoot from an old tree. In Catholic Lauds and in Anglican and Lutheran Morning Prayer, Zechariah's song is still prayed or sung, at the hour when the dayspring actually comes.
screen: then, large: `THE DAYSPRING FROM ON HIGH HATH VISITED US.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: greet the dawn. If it's morning, go to a window or step outside and face the light. If it's not, picture tomorrow's sunrise: the sky going gray, then pale, then gold at the edge. Settle, and breathe. Think of the darkness Zechariah sings about, the shadow some people are sitting in right now. Maybe someone you know. Maybe you. Then let the light come up in your mind, slowly, the way it really does, a little at a time. Light to them that sit in darkness. If you pray, you can greet the morning with Zechariah's words. If you don't, simply watch the light arrive. The bell holds the time.
Benedictus. Latin for blessed, the first word of Zechariah's song when his tongue is loosed, still sung in morning prayer.
Your line: the dayspring from on high. Tomorrow morning, before you check your phone, look at the light for one minute. Let it be the first thing you greet. Day five hundred seven.

508.title: In those days (Luke 2:1–7)
508.hook: an emperor counts his people, and God arrives uncounted
508.howItsDone: Luke 2:1–20 is a Christmas reading in churches, and some families read it aloud at home on Christmas Eve or at the Christmas table.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Benedictus, Zechariah's song when his tongue was loosed. Your line was the dayspring from on high. Did you greet the light this morning before the phone? Day five hundred eight.

Somewhere in Rome, an order goes out. Count everyone, so the empire knows who it can tax. It's the kind of thing powerful people do without thinking twice: a line in a decree, and ordinary lives rearranged. Families pack up and go, each to their own city, to be registered. And among them, walking from Nazareth in Galilee to Bethlehem in Judea, are Joseph, of the house of David, and Mary, the young woman he's engaged to, who is great with child. The emperor will never hear their names. He's counting heads, not looking at faces.

Luke opens the scene like a history book, in the King James Bible: "And it came to pass in those days, that there went out a decree from Caesar Augustus, that all the world should be taxed." Caesar Augustus, emperor of Rome. Some readers puzzle over how this census fits other records of the time, and Luke doesn't stop to explain. He's more interested in the contrast. The emperor's decree moves Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem, David's town, little Bethlehem from Micah, without the emperor ever knowing. Then, in just two verses, the birth itself: "she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn." That's it. No angels yet, no star, no description of the night. A feeding trough for a crib. And notice what isn't there. There's no innkeeper in the story. Nobody slams a door. Luke's Greek word for inn is the same one he uses later for the guestchamber where Jesus eats the Passover with his friends. So some scholars picture a family house with its guest room already full, and the baby laid where the animals fed. Readers notice the shape of it. The emperor sits at the center of the world, counting. And in the Christian telling, God arrives at its edge, uncounted, in a crowded place, in a feeding trough. Some see a hint of the end of Luke's story, when his body is wrapped in linen and laid in a tomb hewn in stone.
screen: `THE CENTER COUNTS; GOD COMES TO THE EDGE.`
then, large: `THERE WAS NO ROOM FOR THEM IN THE INN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice the small in the big news. Settle, and breathe. Think of today's headlines, or whatever's been dominating your feed: an election, a market, a war, a celebrity, a policy. Big names, big numbers. Now look underneath. Who are the people at the edges of that story, the ones who'll never be named? A family packing up. A nurse on a night shift. A child somewhere in the crowd. Pick one and hold them in mind for a moment, by face, not by number. If you pray, you can pray for them. If you don't, simply let them matter to you for a minute. The bell holds the time.
Kataluma, Luke's Greek word for a guest room, usually translated inn: the opening of his birth story, where an emperor counts the world and Jesus is born at its edge, laid in a manger.
Your line: not counted, but there. Today, when you read the news, look for one person the headline missed, and keep them in mind until evening. Day five hundred eight.

509.title: Good tidings of great joy (Luke 2:8–20)
509.hook: the angel to the shepherds: fear not, a savior is born
509.tomorrow: now let me go in peace
509.howItsDone: Christians read the shepherds' story at Christmas, and the angels' song lives on in the Gloria, sung or said in Sunday worship in some churches, and in Christmas carols.

segments.voice: Yesterday, in those days: an emperor counting the world, and a baby laid in a manger at its edge. Your line was not counted, but there. Who did the headline miss today? Day five hundred nine.

Out in the fields near Bethlehem, a few shepherds are keeping watch over their flock by night. It's dark, and the job is mostly staying awake. Not people anyone would invite to a palace. Not people the emperor's census was thinking about. And then, in the King James Bible: "the angel of the Lord came upon them, and the glory of the Lord shone round about them: and they were sore afraid." Sore afraid. Terrified. The dark field suddenly blazing. And the angel's first words are the ones Zechariah and Mary have already heard.

"Fear not: for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people. For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord." Every phrase is loaded. Good tidings means good news, the very thing the word gospel names. Here it comes to shepherds, about a baby. To all people: not just the important ones. This day: tonight, not someday later. And the sign isn't a palace or a crown. "Ye shall find the babe wrapped in swaddling clothes, lying in a manger." The sign is how ordinary he is. Then the sky fills with a multitude of angels praising God and saying: "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men." That line opens the Gloria, a hymn still sung in churches. And here's a curiosity: compare Bibles and the end of the line varies. The King James says peace, good will toward men. Other translations say peace among people with whom God is pleased. The meaning shifts a little either way. Then the shepherds do the simplest thing: "Let us now go even unto Bethlehem, and see." They find everything just as they were told, they spread the word, and people wonder at it. And then a quiet line about Mary: "But Mary kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart." The shepherds broadcast. Mary treasures. Both are ways of receiving good news. Then the shepherds return, the text says, glorifying and praising God. Back to the same sheep, praising as they go.
screen: `THE SIGN IS HOW ORDINARY HE IS.`
then, large: `GOOD TIDINGS OF GREAT JOY, TO ALL PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: tell someone good news. Settle, and breathe. First, find some. Not the big kind, necessarily. Something good that's actually true: a friend's recovery, a kindness you saw, a baby born, a small win at work, a thing you're grateful for. Let it come up and sit with it, the way Mary pondered. Then think of who needs to hear it. Someone who's been surrounded by bad news lately. Someone who'd smile. Picture telling them, the way the shepherds did, a little breathless, not polished. If you pray, you can give thanks for the good news first. If you don't, simply enjoy it before you share it. The bell holds the time.
Evangelist. The English word that comes from the angel's own verb, to announce good news, first spoken to shepherds in a dark field.
Your line: great joy for all people. Today, tell someone the good news you found, and let your face show it. Day five hundred nine.

510.title: Now let me go in peace (Luke 2:21–35)
510.hook: Simeon holds the child and says he can die content; Mary is told a sword will pierce her soul
510.howItsDone: Christians in many traditions say or sing the Nunc Dimittis at the end of the day, at Compline or Evensong, and many churches keep February 2 as the Presentation of the Lord, also called Candlemas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the shepherds heard the angel's evangelist-word on the night shift. Your line was great joy for all people. Who did you tell your good news to? Day five hundred ten.

Forty days after the birth, Joseph and Mary carry the baby up to the temple in Jerusalem, to do what the law of Moses asked of new parents. Luke tells us what they brought as an offering: a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons. That's a detail worth catching. The law allowed birds instead of a lamb for families who couldn't afford one. So this is a poor couple, in the crowded temple courts, with a newborn. Nobody is paying them any attention. Except one man. He's been waiting a long time for this exact moment, and he walks straight toward them.

His name is Simeon. In the King James Bible, he was "just and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel: and the Holy Ghost was upon him." It had been revealed to him that he would not die before he saw the Lord's Christ. So he takes the baby in his arms, and he sings. "Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace, according to thy word: For mine eyes have seen thy salvation." In Latin, it begins Nunc dimittis, now you dismiss, and that's its name. The Greek verb is the one used for releasing a servant from duty, or relieving a watchman at the end of his shift. Simeon has been standing watch his whole life. Now he's off duty. He can go home in peace. And he calls the child "A light to lighten the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel." Both. For the nations and for his own people. A quick surprise here: Luke never says Simeon was old. We assume it because he's ready to die, and artists have always painted him with a white beard. The text just says he was waiting. Then he turns to Mary, and the song changes key. This child will cause the fall and rising of many, a sign that people will speak against, and then: "Yea, a sword shall pierce through thy own soul also." In the middle of the blessing, a warning. Christians have long heard in it the cross, and Mary standing near it. Catholic devotion remembers this as the first of Mary's sorrows. Joy and grief in one embrace, in a crowded temple, over a poor family's child.
screen: then, large: `NOW LETTEST THOU THY SERVANT DEPART IN PEACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: end the day by saying Simeon's words. Right now, settle, and breathe, and look back over today. What did your eyes see that was good? A face, a kindness, a moment of light, even a small one. Name it. What are you still standing watch over, still carrying? Notice it, and imagine setting it down for the night, like a watchman going off duty. Tonight, before you sleep, if you pray, you can say Simeon's words: Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace, according to thy word. If you don't, simply let the day be finished, and let yourself rest. The bell holds the time.
Nunc dimittis. Latin for now you dismiss: Simeon's song, holding the child, ready to go in peace because his eyes have seen.
Your line: depart in peace. Tonight, before sleep, name one good thing your eyes saw today, and then go off duty. Day five hundred ten.

511.title: Anna, eighty-four (Luke 2:36–40)
511.hook: a widow who never left the temple speaks of the child to all who waited
511.howItsDone: Anna is remembered with Simeon at the feast of the Presentation on February 2 in some churches, and Orthodox and Catholic Christians honor her as a saint.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nunc dimittis: Simeon held the child and was ready to go off duty. Your line was depart in peace. What good thing had your eyes seen by bedtime? Day five hundred eleven.

Some congregations have a woman like this. She's been there longer than anyone. She knows where the spare candles are kept. She was praying in that pew before the current pastor was born. She's buried a husband, maybe more than one friend, and she keeps coming, early, every time the doors open. Visitors walk right past her. And she's often the one who notices when something real is happening. Luke has just told us about Simeon. Now, in the same temple, in that same instant, he introduces her ancient counterpart, in three short verses.

In the King James Bible: "And there was one Anna, a prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Aser." Aser is Asher, one of the tribes of Israel. And Anna is the Greek form of Hannah, the same name as the Hannah whose song echoed in Mary's. Luke tells us she was married only seven years, and then: "she was a widow of about fourscore and four years, which departed not from the temple, but served God with fastings and prayers night and day." Fourscore and four is eighty-four. And here's the puzzle: even in English, the line can be read two ways. She was eighty-four years old, or she'd been a widow for eighty-four years, which would make her far older. Translations differ. Either way, years of the same faithful routine, in the same place, waiting. Then: "she coming in that instant gave thanks likewise unto the Lord, and spake of him to all them that looked for redemption in Jerusalem." That instant. After all those years, her timing is perfect. And look what she does. Simeon sings and blesses. Anna talks. She goes around telling everyone who's been waiting like her. In a way she's one of the first people in Luke to tell others about Jesus. Some readers notice Luke pairing a man and a woman: Zechariah and Mary, Simeon and Anna. Then the family goes home to Nazareth, and the child grows strong, filled with wisdom, the grace of God upon him. This week has been crowded with people waiting: Mary's yes, Mary's song, Zechariah's Benedictus, the census, the shepherds, Simeon. And Anna, who never stopped.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank an old woman of faith. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind an older woman whose faithfulness shaped you, or someone near you. A grandmother who prayed for you. A neighbor who always asked how you were. A teacher, a nun, an aunt, the woman at church who remembered your name. She doesn't have to share your beliefs; she just has to be someone who kept showing up. Picture her face, her hands, the place you'd usually find her. Let yourself be grateful for the years she gave. If you pray, you can give thanks for her by name. If you don't, simply hold her in gratitude, and decide how you'll tell her, or how you'll honor her memory. The bell holds the time.
